title: Lifetime, ownership and RAII

objectives.text: Trace object and observer lifetimes across scopes and ownership transfer without using a dangling pointer or equating scope with dynamic allocation lifetime.
Explain and test resource cleanup through RAII on normal scope exit and handled exception unwinding, distinguishing ownership from raw observation and cleanup from transaction rollback.

blocks.markdown: An object has a lifetime: broadly, appropriately sized/aligned storage and completed initialization begin it, and destruction or storage release/reuse can end it, subject to language-specific cases. A name being in scope is not enough to make every object it once referred to alive. An automatic local object normally lives until its scope is left; a dynamically allocated object can outlive the local pointer variable if another owner retains it. This lesson avoids manual placement/reuse/union exceptions and teaches ordinary initialized objects.

An owner is responsible for the resource lifetime. An observer accesses an existing resource but must not outlive it. C++ raw pointer/reference syntax does not itself encode ownership: the Core Guidelines convention treats ordinary T*/T& parameters as non-owning unless an explicit legacy contract says otherwise. A raw pointer can be null; an ordinary reference must refer to a suitable object when bound and cannot be reseated. Neither automatically extends an arbitrary target lifetime or checks validity at each access. Prefer a plain scoped value when dynamic lifetime/indirection is unnecessary.

RAII binds resource ownership to an initialized object whose destructor releases it: memory, a file handle, a lock or a registration can use this pattern. On ordinary scope exit, and when a handled exception unwinds fully constructed automatic objects, destructors release their resources in reverse construction order within the relevant scope. A failed constructor does not run the destructor of the never-fully-constructed object, but already-constructed bases/members are cleaned up. Acquire resources into RAII members rather than leaving a raw handle unprotected across a later throwing operation.

blocks.title: Count live ownership tokens without touching a dead object

steps.text: Initially live=0. Construct outer: 1. Enter the nested block and construct inner: 2.
Leaving the nested block destroys inner and restores 1. Throwing the stated exception then unwinds outer before reaching the surrounding catch, restoring 0.

The counter is synthetic bookkeeping, not an operating-system handle. Deleted copy/move operations prevent accidentally making multiple bookkeeping owners. The example demonstrates lifetime cleanup, not rollback of arbitrary external effects.

blocks.markdown:
Read the class before tracing cleanup

`class ScopeToken { ... };` defines a new type. The final semicolon belongs to the class definition. `public:` makes the following members accessible to callers; it is not a function. `ScopeToken outer;` later creates one local object of this type. Its constructor, `ScopeToken()`, has the same name as the class and no return type. Its body runs when that object is initialized. `++live` increments the counter. The destructor, `~ScopeToken()`, also has no return type; `--live` decrements it when that object's lifetime ends on the shown paths. Do not call the destructor by hand in this example. `noexcept` declares that no exception may escape that destructor; it does not mean every destructor body is automatically safe.

`static int live;` declares one class-wide counter, rather than a separate counter in each token. `int ScopeToken::live = 0;` defines and initializes that shared counter outside the class; `ScopeToken::live` names it through the class. The counter is only this example's bookkeeping, not a built-in lifetime monitor or a thread-safe global statistic.

The four declarations ending in `= delete` forbid the listed copy/move construction and assignment operations. Here `delete` does not free memory. `const ScopeToken&` is a read-only lvalue-reference parameter in the copy forms; `ScopeToken&&` is the rvalue-reference parameter in the move forms. `operator=` names assignment, and its leading `ScopeToken&` is the declared return type. You need not implement these operations to follow the trace: an attempted matching copy/move is rejected by the compiler, which keeps this small counter example from acquiring accidental extra owners.

Read `try { ... } catch (const std::runtime_error&) { ... }` as a protected block and a handler for that exception type by read-only reference. The handler does not need a parameter name. `throw std::runtime_error("synthetic failure");` leaves the normal path. For this handled exception, fully constructed local tokens in the exited scopes are destroyed before the handler runs. Check your reading against the earlier worked trace and the program: explain the counter after construction of outer, construction/destruction of inner, and entry to catch. The trace already supplies these values; this is explanation practice, not an unseen prediction. This bridge explains the existing source; it adds no new runtime or production guarantee.

Syntax references: [constructors](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/constructor.html), [destructors](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/destructor.html), [deleted functions](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/function.html), [exception handlers](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/try.html). Read only the C++20 behavior used here; the references also describe other language versions.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 on separate lines. Fully constructed nested objects are destroyed on the shown exits before control reaches the handler. The destructor only decrements a small bounded synthetic count and is noexcept. No dead object is dereferenced and no crash/abort/process-kill cleanup guarantee is inferred.

blocks.markdown: std::unique_ptr<T> is a standard owning handle for a dynamically allocated T with its associated deleter. make_unique constructs the object and returns its owner. Copying the owner is disabled; moving transfers ownership. After moving the unique_ptr in this example, the source is empty and the destination owns the same Position object at the same address. std::move is a cast enabling move-aware operations, not itself a request to relocate the managed Position. Other moved-from types need their own contracts; do not generalize unique_ptr emptiness to every type.

Read the owning handle without confusing syntax and lifetime

`struct Position { ... };` defines another type. Unlike `class`, its members are public by default. Each Position has its own `int shares`, while `static int destroyed` is one shared counter. `explicit Position(int value) : shares{value} {}` constructs the member directly from value before the empty constructor body runs. `explicit` prevents implicit conversions using this constructor; direct construction by `make_unique<Position>(7)` is still allowed. `~Position()` counts destruction of the Position, not destruction of every pointer that mentions it.

`std::unique_ptr<Position>` is a library handle type parameterized by the managed type. `auto owner = std::make_unique<Position>(7);` deduces that handle type, constructs one Position with shares 7 and gives owner sole ownership. `Position* observer = owner.get();` declares a raw pointer to the same Position without transferring ownership. `observer->shares` reads the member through that pointer, so it requires a live target. The arrow does not check lifetime for you.

`auto next_owner = std::move(owner);` enables the unique_ptr move constructor: ownership transfers, but this Position itself does not move. `nullptr` is the null-pointer value. Comparing owner with nullptr tests whether that handle is empty. `std::boolalpha` changes stream formatting so Boolean values print as true/false. `next_owner.reset()` disposes of its currently owned Position and makes the handle empty. The preceding `observer = nullptr;` only stops this particular observer from retaining the old address; other aliases would not change. Trace the two handles and the one Position separately before checking the caption.

Handle reference: [unique_ptr operations and ownership](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/unique_ptr.html). The explicit constructor, static/member, pointer access and formatting syntax are reading aids for the unchanged example, not new mastery or practice mappings.

blocks.caption: Expected output: true, 7, true, 1, 1 on separate lines. The observer remains valid across this unique_ptr ownership transfer because the Position object is not destroyed/moved. The program deliberately stops observing before reset destroys it. Other aliases would not be automatically nulled. Empty owners do not destroy the object again on scope exit, so the total destructor count stays 1.

blocks.markdown: A function returning a pointer or reference to its ordinary local Position leaves the caller an observer to a destroyed object; do not dereference it to see whether it "still works". Returning an owning value or an appropriate unique_ptr can carry the lifetime instead. Likewise a pointer obtained with get() becomes unusable to access the target after its owner resets/destroys it. get() does not release ownership; release() gives up ownership and requires a correct new owner/deleter plan, so this lesson does not call release() or manual delete.

Destructors should not throw during cleanup. Throwing while another exception is unwinding can terminate the program; std::unique_ptr deleter behavior must satisfy its contract. RAII does not undo a submitted order, restore a database transaction, guarantee a buffered write reached disk or clean up after arbitrary process termination. Use explicit error reporting/transaction protocols for those outcomes. Shared ownership is a separate lifetime policy, not a default cure for uncertainty; choose it only when the contract actually requires shared ownership.

Independent transfer: write a function with one scoped ScopeToken and two nested scopes, testing early return and a handled thrown exception. Verify live returns to 0 on both paths. Add a make_unique Position, transfer its owner once and count exactly one destruction without dereferencing an expired observer. Then explain why a pointer/reference to a local variable is unsafe to return even if the compiler accepts the declaration.

Sources: [ordinary object lifetime](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/lifetime.html), [unique_ptr ownership and disposal](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/unique_ptr.html), and [Core Guidelines R.1/R.3/R.5/R.20/R.21](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines.html). These are language/library/design references, not evidence for app execution or production resource protocols.

summary: Object lifetime, scope, ownership and observation are different. RAII releases owned resources on the stated scope/unwinding paths; unique_ptr transfers a single owner without moving its pointee. Observers still need a live target and cleanup is not external transaction rollback.
